etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English biforhand, biforhond, beforehonde, bifornhand, equivalent to before +‎ hand. [13th century. After Old French avant main].

definitions.definition: At an earlier or preceding time.
(obsolete) In comfortable circumstances as regards property; forehanded.
(archaic, often followed by with) In a state of anticipation or preoccupation.

quote.citation: 1670, John Milton, “(please specify the page)”, in The History of Britain, that Part Especially now Call’d England. […], London:  […]  J[ohn] M[acock] for James Allestry, […] , →OCLC:
quote.text: Agricola  […]  resolves to be beforehand with the danger.

quote.citation: 1716 April 17 (Gregorian calendar), Joseph Addison, “The Free-holder: No. 31. Friday, April 6. [1716.]”, in The Works of the Right Honourable Joseph Addison, Esq; […], volume IV, London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], published 1721, →OCLC:
quote.text: The last cited author has been beforehand with me.

quote.citation: 1839, London Medical Gazette: Or, Journal of Practical Medicine:
quote.text: […]  the medical attendant ought to be rather beforehand with the symptoms of excitement, and to diminish the large quantity of wine before they appear.
